people.name: George Attla
people.role: Famous forerunner in the 1970s for breeding dogs specifically for racing success

people.name: Emmitt Peters
people.role: Champion of the 1975 Iditarod who now greets mushers at his hometown checkpoint of Ruby

people.name: Rick Swenson
people.role: Five-time Iditarod champion who moved from Minnesota to Alaska at age 22 and won championships in 1977, 1979, 1981, 1982, and 1991

people.name: Susan Butcher
people.role: Four-time Iditarod champion who won in 1986, 1987, 1988, and 1990; received her famous lead dog Granite from Joe Redington Sr.

people.name: Martin Buser
people.role: Swiss-born musher who won four Iditarod championships in 1992, 1994, 1997, and 2002; broke the sub-11 day barrier in 1992

people.name: Jeff King
people.role: Four-time Iditarod champion from California who moved to Alaska in 1975 and won in 1993, 1996, 1998, and 2006

people.name: Doug Swingley
people.role: Four-time Iditarod champion who won in 1995, 1999, 2000, and 2001; started with a mishmash team including dogs from the pound

people.name: Dallas Seavey
people.role: Six-time Iditarod champion who won in 2012, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2021, and 2024; holds the current speed record

people.name: Mitch Seavey
people.role: Three-time Iditarod champion who won in 2004, 2013, and 2017; set a speed record in 2017 and became the oldest winner

people.name: Lance Mackey
people.role: Four-time Iditarod champion who won in 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010; runs the Comeback Kennel north of Fairbanks

places.name: Denali Park

places.name: Big Lake, Alaska

places.name: Kotzebue, Alaska

dates.event: First long-distance Iditarod Race held; Tom Mercer and Terry Miller had near-death experience on South Fork of the Kuskokwim River
Mary Shields and Lolly Medley became the first two women to complete the Iditarod; severe mountain storm in Alaska Range with -130 wind chill
Norman Vaughan entered race at age 69 and suffered severe frostbite after 10-inch overflow on the Kuskokwim River
Norman Vaughan was lost for 5 days in a blizzard; Native mushers broke trail at Poorman; Rick Swenson's rookie year finishing 10th
Dick Mackey and Rick Swenson were separated by only the tick of a clock for first and second place; Norman Vaughan returned to complete the race
Susan Butcher placed 2nd behind Rick Swenson in his 4th championship race; Herbie Nayokpuk finished 7th after retreating from a storm
Martin Buser broke the sub-11 day barrier and won championship; Bob Ernisse had near-death experience at Solomon Blow Hole
John Baker from Kotzebue became the first Native Alaskan to win the Iditarod since 1976
Mitch Seavey set the fastest time record of 8 days, 3 hours, 40 minutes, and 13 seconds while becoming the oldest winner
Dallas Seavey broke his father's record with a time of 7 days, 14 hours, 8 minutes, and 57 seconds

trueFalse.statement: When Army soldiers on maneuvers tried to clear the trail before the first 1973 race, all six machines made it through successfully.
trueFalse.correction: Only one out of six machines made it the entire way, and storms covered their trails with more snow.

trueFalse.statement: Early Iditarod sleds were large, heavy wooden freighting sleds weighing 80-90 pounds.
trueFalse.correction: These sleds were built for hauling and transporting, not racing, and could weigh 400-500 pounds when fully loaded.

trueFalse.statement: George Attla was a famous forerunner in the 1970s for breeding dogs specifically for racing success.
trueFalse.correction: While most mushers used dogs for both racing and work, Attla focused on breeding for racing.

trueFalse.statement: Native village mushers in early races were focused on winning and competitive edges.
trueFalse.correction: They were more interested in showing other mushers the route, telling stories, and doing the hard work of trailbreaking.

trueFalse.statement: Rick Swenson won the 1978 race by one second over Dick Mackey.
trueFalse.correction: Dick Mackey won by one second over Rick Swenson; they were separated by only the tick of a clock.

trueFalse.statement: Women were not allowed to race in the Iditarod until the 1980s.
trueFalse.correction: Women were never prohibited; two women signed up and completed the race in 1974.

trueFalse.statement: Susan Butcher received her famous lead dog Granite for free from Joe Redington Sr.
trueFalse.correction: Joe offered her the small, scroungy-looking dog for free, and Granite led her to three of her four victories.

trueFalse.statement: Martin Buser broke the sub-11 day barrier and won the championship in 1992.
trueFalse.correction: This was a significant achievement in the evolution of race speeds.

trueFalse.statement: Dallas Seavey has won the Iditarod six times, the most of any musher.
trueFalse.correction: He won in 2012, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2021, and 2024, and holds the current speed record.

trueFalse.statement: Climate change has had no effect on the Iditarod Race.
trueFalse.correction: Low snowfall affects route choices, rivers break early, and there are economic impacts to checkpoint towns when routes change.
